I’m 68 years old, and I’ve farmed my six mu of good flat land in Quzhou County for more than forty years. My children work in Handan city now, so it’s just me and my wife managing the fields. Because I finished high school—more schooling than most men my age around here—I read the county ag extension pamphlets and I understand soil nutrient balances and irrigation scheduling. But I’m also practical: at my age, I don’t take big risks with unfamiliar cash crops that need constant labor or uncertain markets. I stick to the winter wheat–summer maize rotation that this North China Plain land was made for.

My wheat went into the ground last October after rotary tillage, using an improved semi-dwarf variety the county station recommends. Now that it’s greening up, my plan is straightforward. I’ll top-dress nitrogen at green-up and again at jointing, keeping total N around 16 kg per mu, with about 6 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium as base. I’ll irrigate three times this spring and early summer—green-up recovery, jointing/booting, and grain filling—because rainfall alone won’t carry it, but I won’t waste water on unnecessary rounds. Two pesticide applications: a herbicide in early spring and a fungicide/insecticide spray at flag leaf stage to protect against powdery mildew and aphids. I expect around 550 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

Right after wheat harvest in early June, I’ll plant hybrid summer maize directly into the stubble with no-tillage seeding. Saves diesel, preserves soil moisture, and my back isn’t what it used to be. I’ll band fertilizer at sowing and side-dress nitrogen at the V6–V8 stage, totaling about 15 kg N, 5 kg P, and 4 kg K per mu. Maize here depends on the summer rains, but I’ll irrigate twice—once at emergence if it’s dry, and once at filling if the monsoon stalls. Two pesticide rounds: a pre-emergence herbicide and one insecticide targeting Asian corn borer. I’m counting on roughly 600 kg per mu.

I know groundwater is declining, so I’m careful with every cubic meter. I’m not chasing the absolute highest yield; I’m chasing stable profit with labor I can still handle myself. That’s why I buy quality seed, apply fertilizer based on what the crop actually needs, and avoid excessive spraying. It’s a system that has fed my family for decades, and I see no reason to change it now.
